caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000727
attempts.paper_title: Mapping the Neural Dynamics of Locomotion across the Drosophila Brain
attempts.entry_title: Brain-wide neural correlates of walking in Drosophila (Brezovec et al. 2022)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Brezovec, Berger, Druckmann and Clandinin (2022) on dandiset 000727, which holds whole-brain two-photon imaging and ball tracking of nine walking flies. It streams 12 planes of the authors' processed volumes in the Functional Drosophila Atlas for all flies, and tests the voxel correlations with forward and turning velocity, their symmetry, the principal components and the models that predict velocity from them, the demixing of velocity components, and the timing of neural activity relative to behaviour. Region-level results cannot be tested, as the dandiset has no neuropil labels.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Brezovec et al. (2022) from dandiset 000727

outcomes.statement: Nine flies were imaged for 30 minutes each at a volume rate of about 1.8 Hz, with 256 x 128 x 49 voxels of 2.6 x 2.6 x 5 um (about 1.6 million voxels per volume), giving 30,456 volumes in all, while the ball was tracked at 50 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, A novel method for whole-brain imaging in walking Drosophila, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure 1A legend; STAR Methods, Two-Photon Imaging and Behavior Tracking
outcomes.quote: We then employed two-photon imaging with resonant scanning to achieve a volume imaging rate of 1.8 Hz, collecting approximately 1.6M voxels per volume... 1.6M voxels have each been sampled 30,456 times over the course of 4.5 hr and 9 individuals
outcomes.notes: Nine flies, one session each, 3384 volumes per fly (30,456 in all) at 1.8797 Hz, 1,605,632 voxels of 2.61 x 2.61 x 5 um per raw volume, 30.0 minutes per session, FicTrac 90,000 frames at 50 Hz. The subject ids match the nine flies of the paper's code.

outcomes.statement: About 39% of the brain volume correlates with at least one of forward velocity, left and right angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread across the brain, paragraph 1; Figure 2C; Figure S2
outcomes.quote: We observed that signals were widespread, with 39% of the brain volume correlating with at least one of the three behavioral variables
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), single voxels at p < 1e-4, gives 31.1% of the 191,119 in-brain voxels of the 12 planes, below 35.1 to 42.9% and above 19.5%. Reading (b), 6 x 6 blocks at p < 1e-8, gives 53.5% of the same in-brain voxels, above the band. With each fly's behaviour rolled in time, 0.0% pass under either reading. With behaviour sampled at the start of each volume in place of its midpoint, reading (a) gives 39.2%, so the value depends on the neural times, which the dandiset does not hold. The fraction is 0.0 to 7.5% in the outermost planes and 21.0 to 39.1% in the others. Within single flies 2.4 to 19.7% of voxels pass the threshold for 3384 points. Almost no voxel is negatively correlated (at most 0.01% per component).
deviations: Processed volumes in the Functional Drosophila Atlas, not the paper's mean brain; 12 of 91 planes.
Behaviour sampled at the midpoint of each volume, as the dandiset has no per-plane times; the paper used each plane's acquisition time.
Blocks of 6 x 6 voxels in place of the paper's Ward supervoxels for reading (b).
In-brain voxels are those inside the brain in all nine flies; with voxels inside in any fly the fraction is 20.3%.

outcomes.statement: Of the brain volume, about 15% correlates only with forward velocity, 20% with forward velocity and turning, and 4% only with turning; only about 10% of correlated voxels correlate with all three components, so 90% show a tuning preference.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread across the brain, paragraph 1; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: consisted of voxels that correlated only to VF (15% brain volume)... Most voxels that correlated with VR or VL also correlated with VF (20% brain volume), with relatively few correlating only with turning (4% brain volume)... with only 10% of voxels responding indiscriminately to all velocity components
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), VF only 11.9% (expected 15), VF and turning 15.9% (20), turning only 3.2% (4), and 11.5% of correlated voxels correlated with all three (10). None is within its tolerance; the ranking holds and fewer than 20% of correlated voxels correlate with all three, so most show a tuning preference, as the statement says. Under reading (b) VF and turning is 39.4% and all three 32.2%. With behaviour at the start of each volume, reading (a) gives 11.6, 24.1, 3.5 and 25.7%.
deviations: As for fig2c-fraction-correlated.

outcomes.statement: Forward velocity correlations are mirror-symmetric across the midline, while left and right turning correlations are anti-symmetric, with more correlated voxels in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the turn.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread across the brain, paragraph 1; Figure 2D, E
outcomes.quote: VF correlations exhibited strong mirror symmetry across the midline... In contrast, VR and VL correlations were anti-symmetric, with high levels of correlation on the side of the brain that is ipsilateral to the direction of the turn
outcomes.notes: The VF map correlates with its mirror image at r = 0.823. The VL map correlates with the mirrored VR map at 0.672 and with its own mirror at 0.449. Voxels significant for VL are 2.38 times as many in image half A (x < 157) as in half B, and voxels significant for VR 3.2 times as many in half B. Per fly, the VF mirror correlation is 0.166 to 0.580, summed VL correlation is larger in half A in 8 of 9 flies, summed VR correlation larger in half B in 7 of 9, and both in 6 of 9; fly_098 and fly_105 have VR on the same side as VL and fly_099 has VL on the other side. Against the pooled maps of the other eight flies, no fly matches better mirrored for both VL and VR, as a left-right flip would give; 7 of 9 match better unflipped for both. fly_099's VL map matches the mirrored map slightly better (0.158 against 0.190), its VR map clearly does not (0.439 against 0.199). For fly_105 the check does not decide (VL 0.274 against 0.234, VR 0.212 against 0.214), so a flip of that fly is not excluded; it would lower the pooled asymmetry. The ipsilateral part of the statement is not tested; it holds if half A is the fly's left, which the dandiset does not state.
deviations: Mirror about the centre of the FDA's left-right axis (156.5), chosen from the symmetry of the brain mask; the 0.7 threshold for symmetry is a choice of this attempt, made after the prototype run had shown r = 0.82.

outcomes.statement: Behaviour-correlated voxels occupy most neuropils with non-uniform velocity preferences, strongly in the central complex, posterior slopes, vest, superior medial and lateral protocerebrum, higher visual, olfactory and auditory areas and the mushroom body; IPS, AOTU and VES hold turning-only voxels, MB and LAL forward-and-turning, SMP and SIP forward-only.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural encoding of velocity space is widespread across the brain, paragraphs 2 and 3; Results, Distinct topographic maps of locomotor signals exist in multiple brain regions, paragraph 1; Figure 2E-I
outcomes.quote: Although almost all neuropils contained signals that were correlated with behavior, their velocity preferences were highly non-uniform across brain regions (Figure 2E-I).
outcomes.notes: Needs the neuropil of each voxel. The dandiset holds no neuropil labels, atlas or mean brain for the FDA space of its processed volumes, nor the paper's own mean brain and its registered atlas. The FDA and its labels come from a later paper (BIFROST, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.8pk0p2nx1) that the preprint does not use, so they cannot be brought in under the protocol. Dryad holds no deposit of this paper's data.

outcomes.statement: Within neuropils, voxels of different velocity tuning are spatially organized, for example a forward and ipsilateral-turning column in PLP, left and right compartments in IPS, bands in LO, a dorsal-ventral split in LH, layers in FB, alternating turning in PB, glomeruli in NO and medial and lateral compartments in LAL.
outcomes.source: Results, Distinct topographic maps of locomotor signals exist in multiple brain regions, paragraph 2; Figure 3; Figure S3
outcomes.quote: Taking slices through orthogonal planes of each neuropil, we observed clear spatial organization at the sub-neuropil scale (Figure 3; Figure S3).
outcomes.notes: Needs neuropil boundaries; see fig2e-region-fractions.

outcomes.statement: The first principal components of brain-wide activity are structured by behaviour; PC1 is low when the fly is stopped and high otherwise, PC2 increases with forward velocity and not with angular velocity, and PC3 carries the sign of angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive of locomotor velocity, paragraph 2; Figure 4B-D
outcomes.quote: In particular, the value of PC1 was low when the fly was not moving and high otherwise, while PC2 increased with forward velocity but was invariant with respect to angular velocity, and PC3 encoded information about the sign of the angular velocity.
outcomes.notes: All three parts hold under both readings of the threshold. Reading (a); PC1's below-threshold correlation with VF is 0.202 against 0.065 (PC2) and -0.045 (PC3); above the threshold PC2 has the largest correlation with VF (0.272, PC1 0.162, PC3 0.086) and 0.091 and 0.087 with VL and VR; PC3's above-threshold correlations are 0.114 with VL and -0.259 with VR (p = 3.5e-14 and 5.6e-72). Within each fly over all time points, PC1 correlates positively with VF (0.22 to 0.57) and PC3 more with VL than VR, in 9 of 9 flies. PC1 explains 2.22% of block variance.
deviations: PCA of 5363 blocks from 12 planes, not of 98,000 supervoxels from 49 planes.

outcomes.statement: Linear models on the principal components predict forward, left and right velocity on held-out data with average R2 of about 0.3 using 100 PCs, performance improving over the first 100 PCs before declining.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive of locomotor velocity, paragraph 3; Figure 4F, G
outcomes.quote: model performance improved over the first 100 PCs used, before declining as additional PCs were incorporated (Figure 4F). Notably, all three behavioral variables displayed comparable predictability on held-out test data, with average R2 values of approximately 0.3
outcomes.notes: With 100 superfly PCs the median R2 over flies is 0.155 (VF), 0.196 (VL) and 0.212 (VR); the means are 0.038, 0.155 and 0.178. None is within 0.27 to 0.33; all medians are at least 0.15. Mean R2 rises to 100 PCs and declines after for each component, as stated. Three flies have negative VF R2 (-0.307, -0.306, -0.503). Variants; interleaved folds give medians 0.318, 0.252 and 0.271; alpha chosen within the training folds 0.134, 0.180, 0.212; each fly's own PCs 0.151, 0.210, 0.217. With behaviour rolled in time R2 is at most -0.002. With interleaved folds two of the three medians fall in the band (VF 0.318, VR 0.271; VL 0.252), so the folds, which the paper does not state, account for much of the gap; the outcome would stay partial.
deviations: Five contiguous folds within each fly, a choice; the code does not show its folds.
Alpha is chosen by the best held-out score, as the code does, which selects on the test folds.
The 1000 and 2000 PC models were not run (at most 500 PCs).
PCs of 5363 blocks from 12 planes.

outcomes.statement: Flies that moved less along a velocity component were poorly predicted (R2 near 0), while flies that explored it more were well predicted, with R2 up to 0.6.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive of locomotor velocity, paragraph 3; Figure 4H
outcomes.quote: comparing model predictions on individual animals revealed that flies that moved less along a given velocity component were poorly predicted (R2 of approximately 0), while those that explored a velocity component more were well predicted (with R2 values up to 0.6)
outcomes.notes: The Spearman correlation of a fly's mean amount of a component with its R2 is positive for all three components (VF 0.017, VL 0.383, VR 0.683, p = 0.042 for VR only); the pooled within-component rank correlation is 0.361 with p = 0.064. The largest R2 is 0.534 (fly_094, VF), just below 0.54 to 0.66, and the smallest -0.503. Partially reproduced under the clause that the correlation is positive for at least two components.
deviations: Rests on the R2 of fig4fg-ridge-r2, with its contiguous folds.

outcomes.statement: The model weights given to each PC are stereotyped across flies; PC1 is used for all components, PC2 mainly for forward velocity, and PC3 for left and right turning with opposite signs.
outcomes.source: Results, Neural activity in the central brain is highly predictive of locomotor velocity, paragraph 3; Figure 4I
outcomes.quote: the weights assigned to each PC for each fly, and for each behavior, were highly stereotyped... PC1 was used to predict all velocity components, PC2 was predominantly used to predict forward velocity, and PC3 was used for left and right turning predictions, flipping sign between the two.
outcomes.notes: Median correlation of the weights on PCs 1 to 20 between pairs of flies is 0.646 (VF), 0.732 (VL) and 0.761 (VR). PC3's weight is positive for VL and negative for VR in 9 of 9 flies, PC2's weight is largest for VF in 7 of 9, and PC1's weights have one sign for all three components in 9 of 9. With each fly's behaviour rolled in time (20 rolls), the median pair correlation is at most 0.151, PC3 has opposite signs in 3 to 8 of 9 flies and PC1 one sign in 0 to 6 of 9. Part (iv) follows in part from PC1's orientation, signed to correlate positively with VF, with which it also correlates positively with VL and VR (0.222 and 0.188).
deviations: Weights from a ridge fit to all of each fly's time points at the alpha chosen in fig4fg-ridge-r2, with each component scaled to unit s.d.

outcomes.statement: Demixing with linear models shows that forward velocity is uniquely encoded by a spatially organized subset of voxels, while locomotor state (walking or stopped) is not uniquely encoded anywhere, although the single-variable maps of forward velocity and locomotor state are very similar.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution of each velocity component to neural activity, paragraph 2; Figure 5A
outcomes.quote: while the single variable forward walking and locomotor state (stopped versus walking) maps were very similar, the maps created by demixing revealed that forward velocity was encoded by a spatially organized subset of voxels, while locomotor state was not encoded uniquely anywhere in the brain.
outcomes.notes: At the 0.01 threshold, 5 blocks (0.09%) encode walking state uniquely and 40 (0.75%) encode VF uniquely, 8 times as many, but fewer than the 5% the criterion requires. Unique contributions are small everywhere (largest 0.032 for VF, 0.012 for walking state) and the full model's median held-out R2 is 0.0019. The single-variable maps of VF and walking state correlate at 0.882 over blocks, as the statement says. At a threshold of 0.005 walking state is unique in 1.88% of blocks and VF in 2.24%; with the walking state the code intended, in 0.97% and 0.91%, so the VF advantage depends on the 0.01 threshold, which lies far above the median full-model R2, and on the definition of walking state. Within single flies walking state is unique in up to 8.35% of blocks (fly_094).
deviations: Ridge alpha 1 on behaviour scaled to unit s.d., folds as fifths of every fly, and the 0.01 threshold are choices; the Methods give none of them.
Walking state as the code computes it, which uses forward velocity alone.
Blocks in place of supervoxels.

outcomes.statement: The functional regions defined by the unique contributions of forward, left and right velocity are all correlated with velocity when the fly is below the movement threshold, a widespread increase in activity at the initiation of movement, while above the threshold each region correlates most with its own velocity component.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution of each velocity component to neural activity, paragraph 3; Figure 5B, C; Figure S5B
outcomes.quote: we found that all three regions were highly correlated when the fly was stopped (below the threshold), strongly arguing for a wide-spread increase in neural activity associated with the initiation of movement... each region had strong correlations with only one behavioral velocity component.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b) of the threshold all nine below-threshold correlations of the forward, left and right regions (40, 4 and 8 blocks) with the three components are positive with p < 0.05 (0.013 to 0.221), and above the threshold each region correlates most with its own component (0.377, 0.170, 0.266). Under reading (a) the left region with VR is -0.008 (p = 0.2), so only reading (b) satisfies the criterion. The Pearson p-values treat time points as independent; against 200 rolls of each fly's behaviour in time, which keep the autocorrelation, all nine are above chance under reading (b), the weakest (left region with VR, r = 0.013) with p = 0.025 against a null 95th percentile of 0.010. The left region holds only 4 blocks.
deviations: Regions are the few blocks with a unique contribution of at least 0.01 in fig5a-unique-variance.
The threshold readings are two interpretations of the 0.75 s.d. of Figure 4E.

outcomes.statement: When the fly turns, neural activity increases in specific regions of the ipsilateral hemisphere and decreases in the same regions of the contralateral hemisphere.
outcomes.source: Results, Demixing the unique contribution of each velocity component to neural activity, paragraph 4; Figure 5F
outcomes.quote: the demixing linear model revealed that when the fly is turning, neural activity on the ipsilateral hemisphere increases in specific regions, while the contralateral hemisphere experiences a corresponding decrease in activity in the same regions (Figure 5F).
outcomes.notes: Turning raises activity mostly on one side, opposite for the two directions (82% of the top 10% of blocks in half A for left turns, 25% for right turns), but the mirror blocks rise as well; their median change against slow walking is +0.0064 for left turns and +0.0022 for right turns, and 36% and 42% of them fall. The same holds with turning thresholds of 50 and 150 deg/s, and in 8 of 9 flies for left turns and 9 of 9 for right turns. With the change predicted by the demixing model of fig5a-unique-variance, as the paper derives Figure 5F, the mirror blocks rise as well (medians 0.0254 and 0.0111; 6.5% and 18.8% fall), as do the model's VL and VR coefficients of the mirror blocks (median 0.0064). The ipsilateral increase holds; the contralateral decrease does not.
deviations: The bounds for slow walking (1 to 3 mm/s, below 30 deg/s) and turning (beyond 100 deg/s) are choices; the paper does not state its own.
Neural activity and behaviour at the same volume time, without a lag.
The main test compares mean activity in turns and slow walking; the paper uses the demixing model, shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The time of peak cross-correlation between supervoxel activity and forward velocity ranges from about 300 ms before the change in behaviour, the earliest, to more than 1 s after it.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior varies across brain regions, paragraph 1; Figure 6A-E
outcomes.quote: the earliest correlations between neural activity and behavior emerged in specific neuropils approximately 300 milliseconds before the change in behavior, with the latest peak correlations persisting for more than 1 second after the change in behavior.
outcomes.notes: Reading (b); the 99th percentile of VF lead over the 2145 top blocks is 0.32 s, within 0.27 to 0.33 s, and the 1st percentile a lag of 1.23 s. Reading (a) gives an earliest lead of 0.44 s (outside tolerance) and a latest lag of 1.44 s. VL and VR give 99th percentiles of 0.30 and 0.22 s and 1st percentiles of lags of 1.24 and 1.22 s. With volume-start times the VF 99th percentile is 0.58 s. The median VF lead changes steadily with FDA plane from 0.36 s (plane 17) to -0.30 s (plane 80), a spread of 0.66 s against a volume period of 0.532 s, the pattern unknown plane acquisition times would produce; the dandiset gives neither the times nor the order of the planes. With each plane's median removed the 99th percentile is 0.50 s and the 1st -1.02 s, so the match within 0.03 s is not robust to the neural times; the lag of more than 1 s holds in both (1st percentile at least 0.84 s of lag in every plane from 38 to 80, more than 1 s in planes 59 to 73). Only the lag of more than 1 s is robust; the earliest lead cannot be tested with the timing the dandiset gives, and the outcome follows the criterion fixed in advance. Fitted per fly, the 99th percentile is 0.36 to 4.55 s.
deviations: Neural times at the volume midpoint, an error of up to 0.27 s per block.
Notch filter Q = 2 is a choice; the code's notch coefficients are not in the repository.
Top 40% by peak value of the deconvolved filter.

outcomes.statement: Supervoxels whose peak correlation lags behaviour have broader temporal kernels, while those that anticipate behaviour have narrow kernels.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior varies across brain regions, paragraph 1; Figure 6H
outcomes.quote: we observed a positive correlation between the time of peak correlation and the width of the temporal kernel, i.e. supervoxels that contain delayed information about behavior displayed a broad temporal kernel, while supervoxels that contain anticipatory information about behavior displayed narrow temporal kernels
outcomes.notes: Over the 2145 top VF blocks, lag and FWHM correlate at r = 0.672 (p = 2.2e-281, Spearman 0.703); mean FWHM is 1.38 s for blocks leading by up to 0.5 s and 2.62 s for blocks lagging by more than 1 s. VL and VR give r = 0.442 and 0.449; volume-start times 0.673. The plane means of lag and FWHM correlate at 0.979 over 10 planes, so plane accounts for part of the relation; with plane means removed r = 0.623 (p = 6.3e-231), and within single planes r is positive in all 10 planes with at least 10 blocks (0.222 to 0.751), with p < 0.05 in 8.
deviations: As for fig6-peak-time-range; FWHM measured from 0, around the peak.

outcomes.statement: Across nearly all brain regions, the peak correlation with angular velocity comes first in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the turn, then in the contralateral one.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior varies across brain regions, paragraph 3; Figure 6F, G
outcomes.quote: Finally, across nearly all brain regions, the time of peak correlation with angular velocity emerged first in the ipsilateral hemisphere relative to the contralateral hemisphere.
outcomes.notes: For VL, over 868 mirror pairs, the block in half A leads its partner by a median 0.16 s and is earlier in 67% of pairs; for VR, over 849 pairs, the block in half B leads by 0.14 s and is earlier in 72%; both Wilcoxon p-values print as 0. The median difference is 0.26 to 0.33 s in planes 17 to 38 for VL and 0.19 to 0.29 s in planes 17 to 59 for VR, and -0.03 to 0.03 s in planes 73 and 80. Both blocks of a pair lie in one FDA plane; whether the two halves of a plane were acquired at the same time is not known.
deviations: The ipsilateral half is the image half with more significant correlations for that turn, from fig2-symmetry, since the dandiset does not say which half is left.

outcomes.statement: Peak correlations follow a sequence across regions; for forward velocity the antennal lobe and lateral horn first, then mushroom body, GNG and saddle, the central complex spanning onset, and the optic lobes lagging by up to more than a second; for angular velocity IPS, GOR and VES lead and the central complex and optic lobes lag.
outcomes.source: Results, The temporal relationship between neural activity and behavior varies across brain regions, paragraphs 2 and 3; Figure 6E-G
outcomes.quote: For changes in forward velocity, the earliest peak correlations appeared in olfactory sensory areas, namely the Antennal Lobe (AL) and Lateral Horn (LH)... Thus, changes in forward velocity are correlated with a characteristic sequence of changes in neural activity distributed widely across the brain
outcomes.notes: Needs the neuropil of each supervoxel; see fig2e-region-fractions. The timing would also need the per-plane acquisition times and the paper's z-depth maps, which are not in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Within brain regions, peak correlation times form spatial gradients, for example a dorsal before ventral order in LH for forward velocity and ipsilateral before contralateral order in LAL, MB-ML and PLP for angular velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Individual brain regions display spatiotemporally structured patterns of engagement, paragraph 1; Figure 7; Figure S7
outcomes.quote: These analyses revealed that even within each brain region, the temporal order of neural engagement was highly organized, and aligned with both behavioral and anatomical features.
outcomes.notes: Needs neuropil boundaries (see fig2e-region-fractions) and per-plane acquisition times, neither of which is in the dandiset.

outcomes.statement: Correlations computed from the tdTomato structural channel show no behaviour-related signal, so motion artefacts are undetectably small.
outcomes.source: Figure S2E, H legend
outcomes.quote: The absence of signal in this Figure indicates that motion artifacts were undetectably small.
outcomes.notes: The dandiset holds the tdTomato channel only raw, without motion correction or registration. Repeating the paper's per-volume ANTs SyN motion correction for 30,456 volumes, and the warps to a common space, is also out of reach here (not_runnable). A check on the raw, uncorrected channels (raw planes 18 and 30, high-pass filtered as the code does, within each fly) does not decide the outcome; the median share of voxels correlated with VF, VL or VR at p < 1e-4 is 0.23% for tdTomato and 0.60% for GCaMP6f, tdTomato exceeds GCaMP6f in 5 of 18 fly-planes, and it reaches 3.53% in fly_089, against 0.83% for GCaMP6f.

outcomes.statement: Behaviour prediction peaks at 2000 supervoxels per plane, among 1 to 10,000.
outcomes.source: STAR Methods, Agglomerative Clustering Supervoxel Creation; Figure S4A
outcomes.quote: Too few or too many supervoxels results in lower prediction accuracy, with a peak at 2000 supervoxels (Figure S4A).
outcomes.notes: Needs Ward clustering of every plane of the nine flies pooled at seven cluster numbers, so every voxel of all 91 planes. The 12 planes streamed here are 22.1 GB compressed and took 306 s in the latest run (214 s in the run before), including about 40 s for metadata; all 91 planes are several times that, which leaves no room within the 30 minute limit for the clustering itself. The files total 610 GB. A partial sweep on the 12 streamed planes was not attempted. It would need each plane's voxel time series held in memory (about 27,000 in-brain voxels x 30,456 points, some 3 GB per plane) for Ward clustering at seven sizes, followed by the PCA and ridge models at each size, while the streaming here keeps only block means and per-voxel sums.

findings.statement: The processed volumes are registered into the Functional Drosophila Atlas, but the dandiset holds no neuropil labels, atlas or template for that space, nor the paper's own mean brain and registered atlas. None of the paper's region-level results (Figures 2E to I, 3, 6E to G, 7) can be tested.

The processed series is in the Functional Drosophila Atlas, a space from a later paper of the lab, while the preprint analyses its data in its own mean brain. The dandiset does not say how the FDA series relates to the preprint's analysis space or which preprocessing it shares.

The per-plane acquisition times of the Bruker recordings are not in the files, which give only a volume rate. The paper aligns behaviour to each plane's time. Sampling behaviour at the start in place of the middle of each volume changes the correlated share of the brain from 31.1% to 39.2% and the 99th percentile of forward-velocity lead from 0.32 to 0.58 s.
The supervoxel labels, the z-depth maps used to give each supervoxel its acquisition time, and the motion-corrected tdTomato channel used as the paper's motion control are not deposited.
The processed series has grid spacing 1, 1, 1 in unit "unknown", so its voxel size is not given, and nothing states which half of the volume is the fly's left.

Imaging and FicTrac both start at 0 s; the conversion code set FicTrac timestamps to a uniform 50 Hz from 0 because synchronisation data were missing, and the dandiset does not say so. The data are consistent with a shared start (brain-wide activity follows walking speed by 0.4 to 0.8 s in every fly), to within a few hundred milliseconds.

Every FicTrac SpatialSeries has unit "meters" and conversion 0.0045 (the ball radius), while most hold angles in radians, as their descriptions say (heading, orientations, positions in radians, speed in radians per frame). SpatialSeriesRotationDeltaError, described as an error in radians, has medians of 6067 to 10,435.

The paper's code computes the walking state with np.sqrt(a, b), where b is taken as the output array, so the state reduces to absolute forward velocity over its s.d. above 0.2; the line was written to combine forward and rotational velocity. The two versions mark 47.2% and 57.3% of time points as walking.

The Methods cite Figure 3F and 3G for the PCA model sweep and the per-fly PCs, which are in Figure 4F and 4G. The Results describe Figure 3G as the Nodulus, while the Figure 3 legend calls panel G the Ellipsoid Body.

The preprint says the microscopy and behavioural data were deposited at Dryad and the code at GitHub, with DOIs in a key resources table that the preprint does not include. No Dryad record of these data was found, and the dandiset links neither the analysis code nor Dryad. The analysis code was found as ClandininLab/brezovec_volition_2023, whose README gives a different title.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file. It also checked the blocked claims against the archive's asset list and metadata.

disagreements.reason: The own-component part holds under both readings. The below-threshold part fails under (a): left region vs VR r = -0.008, p = 0.2. Under (b) it passes only on r = 0.013, p = 0.031, and that p-value treats 27,054 autocorrelated samples as independent and would not survive any effective-sample-size correction; the left region is only 4 blocks. It asked for a circular-shift null for the below-threshold correlations.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the revised entry (after round 1), with its conclusion cells and summary, the helper module, the claims file and this record.

entries.name: 000727-brezovec-2022
entries.title: Brain-wide neural correlates of walking in Drosophila (Brezovec et al. 2022)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Brezovec, Berger, Druckmann and Clandinin (2022) on dandiset 000727, which holds whole-brain two-photon imaging and ball tracking of nine walking flies. It streams 12 planes of the authors' processed volumes in the Functional Drosophila Atlas for all flies, and tests the voxel correlations with forward and turning velocity, their symmetry, the principal components and the models that predict velocity from them, the demixing of velocity components, and the timing of neural activity relative to behaviour. Region-level results cannot be tested, as the dandiset has no neuropil labels.
